labs.econ.logitprobit.presets.stdLogit.d: Moderate sample size, strong x1 effect
Data generated by a Probit process
Negative intercept, low share of y=1
labs.econ.logitprobit.coefNote: Note: Logit and Probit coefficients are not directly comparable due to different scales; compare marginal effects instead. Rule of thumb: Logit β̂ ≈ 1.6 × Probit β̂.
labs.econ.logitprobit.marginalEffectsNot: AME = (1/n)Σᵢ f(xᵢ'β)·βₖ; MEM = f(x̄'β)·βₖ. LPM coefficients are direct marginal effects, usually close to AME (often used as a quick approximation).
labs.econ.logitprobit.predictedProbNote: LPM often exceeds the [0,1] interval at the ends (truncated here); Logit and Probit curves overlap significantly, showing minimal fitting differences.
labs.econ.logitprobit.takeaways.linkFnBo: Logit uses the logistic CDF Λ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), while Probit uses the standard normal CDF Φ(z). They differ in tail behavior (Logit has fatter tails).
labs.econ.logitprobit.takeaways.whyNotOl: Heteroskedasticity; predicted probabilities can fall outside [0,1]; constant marginal effects assumption is often unrealistic.
labs.econ.logitprobit.takeaways.marginal: β̂ coefficients lack direct scale meaning; AME or MEM are needed to quantify how a 1-unit increase in x affects the probability (in percentage points).
labs.econ.logitprobit.takeaways.mleBody: Estimated via Newton-Raphson (IRLS) iteration to solve ∂L/∂β = 0; standard errors come from the diagonal of the inverse Fisher Information Matrix I(β̂)⁻¹.
labs.econ.logitprobit.takeaways.pseudoR2: 1 − ll(full) / ll(intercept-only); values between 0.2-0.4 indicate a strong fit in discrete choice models.
